Matching Matching of MHC antigens is critical in most 
transplants. In practice, only A, B, and DR are typed (see
Box 9.8). Th e patient’s blood is also tested for reactivity with the
donor’s lymphocytes to determine if the recipient has antibod-
ies to the donor’s cells and if hyperacute rejection is likely to 
occur. MHC antigens that test as the same serologically are not 
always exactly the same genetically. Family members are often
considered as potential donors. Since the genes for MHC are 
inherited as a unit (haplotype), each individual will share at 
least one A, one B, and one C with each parent; hypothetically,
with three-quarters of his or her siblings; and possibly with 
grandparents, aunts, uncles, and cousins.
Immunosuppression Immunosuppression is required 
both at the time of the transplant and lifelong for the transplant
recipient. Examples of the drugs used to accomplish immuno-
suppression include cortiocosteroids, cyclosporine, and tacro-
limus.18 Th ese medications have numerous side eﬀ ects, some
